title: How a Network Learns
eyebrow: CETI · the two-minute feature · a network learning Fisher's irises · draft A, the laboratory
lede: A two-layer network is shown Fisher's 150 irises. After 10 steps it already gets 135 right; the last 8 cost 208 steps, and the last 769 steps add no flower at all. The flowers as a point cloud in a measured box, the loss as a lit slice the bead runs down, the network as ribbons in a cutaway.

captions: A small network is shown 150 flowers and their names.
After 10 steps, how many does it get right?
Irises measured by Anderson, 1935; Fisher, 1936.
150 flowers, 3 species. 4 measurements, 3 drawn.
Setosa stands apart: no petal longer than 1.9 cm.
Versicolor and virginica: 37 share 4.5–5.1 cm.
4 measurements in, 8 hidden units, 3 names out.
67 weights decide its answers. Errors cost loss.
Two of the weights as ground, loss as height.
1,000 steps downhill, from loss 1.393.
Off the wall at once, then a crawl to 0.039.
The same 150 flowers ride through the network.
Step 0, random weights: 13 land on the right name.
After 10 steps: 135 right. 122 more, in 10 steps.
Step 50: 144. Step 100: 146. Weights thicken.
Step 1,000: 148 of 150. 2 never land right.
Lit = right. 90 % of the loss drop by step 34.
13 to 140 right: 23 steps. The last 8: 208.
Then 769 more steps, and not one more flower.
The 2 misses sit inside the shared band.
Monday: once it goes flat, which cases still miss?
Graded on the 150 it learned from; new flowers untested.

brand.takeaway: Fast at first. The last few cost the most.

sources: Fisher RA. The use of multiple measurements in taxonomic problems. Annals of Eugenics 1936;7(2):179–188. doi:10.1111/j.1469-1809.1936.tb02137.x
Anderson E. The irises of the Gaspé Peninsula. Bulletin of the American Iris Society 1935;59:2–5.
Fisher RA. Iris [dataset]. UCI Machine Learning Repository, 1988. doi:10.24432/C56C76; Bezdek JC et al. Will the real iris data please stand up? IEEE Trans Fuzzy Systems 1999;7(3):368–369.
factory/topics/how-a-network-learns/recompute.py (numpy, seed 0; run --check to re-derive every S4 claim).
Rumelhart DE, Hinton GE, Williams RJ. Learning representations by back-propagating errors. Nature 1986;323:533–536.
Li H, Xu Z, Taylor G, Studer C, Goldstein T. Visualizing the loss landscape of neural nets. NeurIPS 2018.
honest: Graded on the 150 it learned from; new flowers untested. One small network, one learning rate, one dataset: it shows how training loss and training accuracy move, not accuracy on unseen data, large models or other optimisers. The ground is a 2-D slice with the other 65 weights held at step 1,000.
